claims.text: The alloying element X governs the nature and stability of the high-temperature oxide scale in CrFeCoNiX HEAs.
Al has sufficiently high oxygen affinity to promote preferential alumina formation in CrFeCoNiAl.
The limited diffusivity of Al drives Al segregation to the alloy surface.
Surface segregation of Al produces a continuous, coherent, low-strain Al2O3 layer.
The resulting Al2O3 layer adheres well to the CrFeCoNiAl substrate.
Mn and Si have lower oxygen affinity and faster diffusion rates than Al in the relevant alloys and exposure regime.
CrFeCoNiMn and CrFeCoNiSi form non-protective, multiphase oxide scales under the stated high-temperature exposure.
The oxide scales formed on the Mn- and Si-containing alloys crack or spall.
Elemental segregation at the oxide/alloy interface governs the interfacial lattice match between the oxide and substrate.
Interfacial lattice match dictates oxide coherency.
The oxygen affinity and diffusion characteristics of X control the kinetics of its surface segregation.
Oxides produced by the Mn- and Si-containing alloys have greater interfacial strain because of poorer lattice matching.
Greater oxide/alloy interfacial strain promotes oxide-scale cracking and spallation.
At 950 °C under otherwise identical exposure conditions, the Al-containing alloy will form a more stable, continuous, coherent, and protective oxide scale than the Mn- or Si-containing alloys.
The proposed comparison varies X among Al, Mn, and Si while controlling fabrication, surface finish, and high-temperature exposure.
The proposed exposure is 950 °C for 50 to 100 hours in air or a defined corrosive gas mixture.
The proposed material state consists of gas-atomized-powder-derived, single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution alloys with uniformly polished surfaces.
The hypothesis is intended to apply around 950 °C in oxidative or mildly corrosive atmospheres and may not apply outside that temperature or atmospheric range.
Failure of the Al-containing alloy to form the specified alumina scale, or formation of similarly coherent and adherent scales on the Mn- or Si-containing alloys, would falsify the hypothesis.
